# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–24 (Complete – Updated 171)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of sixth year** (Chapter 24). Duel between Rawdon and Steyne occurred; outcome resolved without public scandal. Rawdon accepted Coventry Island Governorship (three thousand a year). Little Rawdon remains at school. Amelia continues living at Russell Square, overseeing Georgy's education and relationship with his grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opened "autumn of sixth year"; Chapter 24 opens "winter of sixth year."
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row); Coventry Island (where Rawdon now Governor); Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe hill farms; Bryngate market town.

## The Duel Resolution and Its Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23–24)

**Macmurdo's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: When Rawdon wavered after learning of Coventry Island appointment, Macmurdo rebuked him, insisting affair was placed in his hands. Refused to carry further challenge; argued duel would disgrace all parties. Advised Rawdon to accept Coventry Island position and maintain silence, claiming no proof against Rebecca and that Rawdon would be fool not to accept the appointment.

**Duel Occurred (Chapter 24)**: Secret rencontre occurred between Rawdon and Steyne; principals and seconds agreed to bury outcome "in the profoundest oblivion."

**Town Gossip Erupts (Chapter 24)**: Despite sworn secrecy, story spread rapidly across London within hours—Little Cackleby attended seven evening parties telling story with "comments and emendations." Mrs. Washington White "revelled in it." Bishopess of Ealing shocked; Bishop visited Gaunt House. Lady Jane (Southdown) sympathetic; Lady Southdown wrote news to daughter at Cape of Good Hope. **Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Mr. Wagg acting on Wenham's hint**—duel remained town-talk for three days but kept from press.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation (Chapter 24)**: Pitt attempted to convey message that "affair all right between Lord Steyne and the Colonel." Rawdon refused: Rebecca concealed money from him ten years; she swore she had none from Steyne, but "directly I found it" she knew "it was all up." Rawdon declared: "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty, and I'll never see her again--never."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship (Chapter 24)**: Initially resisted appointment "procured for him by so odious a patron" (Steyne). Persuaded to accept by Pitt's entreaties and mainly Macmurdo's argument that Steyne would be "in a fury" if enemy's fortune was made through his means—accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Final Dissolution (Chapter 24)

**Household Seized**: Bailiffs and brokers seized Raggles's property in Curzon Street. Rebecca's fate immediately after unknown—"where? Who cared!"

**Rumors and Speculation**: World divided on guilt; rumors proliferated across European locations (Naples, Palermo, Bierstadt, Boulogne, Cheltenham). Narrative comment: "We all know how charitable the world is, and how the verdict of Vanity Fair goes when there is a doubt."

**Financial Arrangements**: Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity"—she possessed talent for "making a little money go a great way."

## Rawdon's Life in Coventry Island (Chapter 24)

**Colonial Governance**: Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand a year. Sent Macmurdo cigars; sent Lady Jane colonial produce (shells, cayenne pepper, hot pickles, guava jelly). Sent brother Swamp Town Gazette, where new Governor praised with "immense enthusiasm" in one paper, called "a tyrant, compared to whom Nero was an enlightened philanthropist" in another. Little Rawdon enjoyed reading papers about his Excellency.

**Obligations Maintained**: Remitted to Pitt punctually; wrote to little Rawdon regularly every mail. Cannot obtain life insurance (island climate too dangerous) to pay debts on leaving England.

**Moral Regeneration**: Complete transformation accomplished. Maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education and future, compensates those wronged (Briggs via Pitt), and accepts prosperity gained through enemy's patronage as ironic justice and quiet revenge.

## Georgy Osborne's Establishment and Education (Chapter 24)

**Current Status and Household**: Georgy "fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square, occupant of his father's room in the house and heir apparent of all the splendours there." Mr. Osborne (grandfather) "as proud of him as ever he had been of the elder George"—boy's "good looks, gallant bearing, and gentlemanlike appearance" won grandsire's heart.

**Intellectual Superiority**: Grandfather asked Georgy daily what he studied, making "a hundred blunders" revealing ignorance. Georgy's "quick brain and better education elsewhere showed the boy very soon that his grandsire was a dullard." Boy "began accordingly to command him and to look down upon him."

**Amelia's Lasting Influence (Chapter 24)**: Georgy's previous education under Amelia made "a much better gentleman of Georgy than any plans of his grandfather could make him." Amelia described as: "kind, weak, and tender woman, who had no pride about anything but about him, and whose heart was so pure and whose bearing was so meek and humble that she could not but needs be a true lady...gentle offices and quiet duties...never said brilliant things...never spoke or thought unkind ones; guileless and artless, loving and pure." Assessment: "Indeed how could our poor little Amelia be other than a real gentlewoman!"

**The Miniature Gift (Chapter 24)**: Georgy visits Amelia regularly at Brompton, "galloping down the little street" in splendid new white great-coat with cape and velvet collar. Amelia replaced his humble homemade shirts and neckcloths with fine linen from Miss Osborne (humble items given to coachman's boy), but she "tried to think she was pleased at the change" and was "happy and charmed to see the boy looking so beautiful." She hung little black profile of him by side of another portrait over her bed.

Georgy brought red morocco case containing miniature portrait of himself—commissioned by grandfather's artist in Southampton Row. Georgy paid painter from own money to create copy, wanting to give it to his mother. Old Osborne, pleased by incident, gave boy twice sovereigns paid for miniature.

**Amelia's Ecstasy**: Proof of boy's affection charmed Amelia so she thought "no child in the world was like hers for goodness." Thought of his love made her happy "for long weeks after." Slept with picture under pillow; kissed and wept and prayed over it "many many times." "A small kindness from those she loved made that timid heart grateful. Since her parting with George she had had no such joy and consolation."

**Physical Appearance and Dress**: Scarcely eleven years old; wore straps and beautiful little boots "like a man," gilt spurs, gold-headed whip, fine pin in handkerchief, neatest kid gloves. Famous tailor Mr. Woolsey of Conduit Street (West End) summoned; Mr. Osborne scorned City or Holborn tailors. Woolsey created fancy trousers, waistcoats, jackets, white waistcoats for evening parties, cut velvet waistcoats for dinners, "dear little darling shawl dressing-gown, for all the world like a little man." Dressed for dinner every day "like a regular West End swell." One domestic specially attended him at toilette, answered his bell, brought letters on silver tray.

**Daily Habits and Precocity**: After breakfast, sat in arm-chair in dining-room reading Morning Post "just like a grown-up man." Servants delighted: "How he DU dam and swear." Those remembering Captain his father "declared Master George was his Pa, every inch of him." Made house lively "by his activity, his imperiousness, his scolding, and his good-nature."

**Friendships and Entertainments**: Young Todd of Coram Street, Russell Square, was Master George's great friend and admirer. Both had taste for painting theatrical characters, hardbake and raspberry tarts, sliding and skating in Regent's Park and Serpentine (weather permitting), attending plays. Rowson, Master George's appointed body-servant, conducted them to theatres; they sat in great comfort in pit. Visited principal theatres of metropolis; knew names of all actors from Drury Lane to Sadler's Wells; performed many plays to Todd family and youthful friends using West's famous characters on pasteboard theatre. Rowson, generous disposition, treated young master to oysters after play and glass of rum-shrub for night-cap when in cash. Master George's "liberality and gratitude for the pleasures" likely profited Rowson in turn.

## Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Chapter 24, Excerpts 1416–1423)

**Institution and Pupils**: School located Hart Street, Bloomsbury. Veal domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Institution has four boarding pupils: West Indian gentleman with "mahogany complexion" and "woolly head" with "exceedingly dandyfied appearance" (no visitors); hulking boy of three-and-twenty with neglected education being introduced to polite world; two sons of Colonel Bangles of East India Company's Service. Georgy is day boy only, arrives mornings under guardianship of Rowson, rides away afternoons on pony followed by groom (weather permitting). Georgy's grandfather's wealth "reported in the school to be prodigious."

**Veal's Method and Character**: Advertised system "prepared young noblemen and gentlemen for the Universities, the senate, and the learned professions" without "degrading corporal severities still practised at the ancient places of education," offering "elegances of refined society and the confidence and affection of a home." Veal compliments Georgy personally on wealth and destined high station; warns him to prepare through "sedulity and docility in youth" for lofty duties; reminds him "obedience in the child was the best preparation for command in the man"; begs George not bring toffee to school as it ruins health of Masters Bangles. **Notable failing**: Veal frequently late Georgy's arrival and defaulting behavior but does not impose consequences.

**Curriculum**: Claimed to be "of prodigious extent"—boys could learn "something of every known science." Veal possessed: orrery, electrifying machine, turning lathe, theatre (in wash-house), chemical apparatus, "select library of all the works of the best authors of ancient and modern times and languages." Took boys to British Museum; descanted upon antiquities and natural history specimens so audiences gathered round him and "all Bloomsbury highly admired him as a prodigiously well-informed man."

**Veal's Speech Habits**: Spoke "almost always," deliberately employed "very finest and longest words" of vocabulary, believing "it was as cheap to employ a handsome, large, and sonorous epithet, as to use a little stingy one."

**Specific Dialogue Example**: Veal remarks to George about illuminated windows at "venerated grandfather's almost princely mansion in Russell Square" and inquires if Mr. Osborne entertained "chosen spirits" at "sumptuous board." Asserts guests "had no reason to complain of their repast"; boasts of his own invitations to Osborne's table; references patron "Right Honourable George Earl of Bareacres"; claims merchant's board "to the full as richly served" and "reception as gratifying and noble" as feasts with great and noble; interrupts lesson with Eutropis passage, noting Georgy's late arrival and prior defaulting.

**Progress Reports**: Weekly reports to grandfather list score or more branches of knowledge with pupil's progress marked by professor. Georgy marked: aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French, et cetera. "Everybody had prizes for everything at the end of the year"—even Mr. Swartz (woolly-headed West Indian, half-brother to Honourable Mrs. Mac Mull), Mr. Bluck (neglected three-and-twenty-year-old from agricultural district), and "idle young scapegrace" Master Todd received "little eighteen-penny books, with 'Athene' engraved on them, and a pompous Latin inscription from the professor."

**Amelia's Involvement**: Bewildered by Veal's phrases but thought him "prodigy of learning." Made friends with Mrs. Veal "for reasons of her own"—liked to be in house seeing Georgy come to school there. Attended Mrs. Veal's monthly conversazioni (pink cards with "AOHNH" [Greek goddess Athene] engraved on them) where professor welcomed pupils and friends to "weak tea and scientific conversation." "Poor little Amelia never missed one of these entertainments and thought them delicious so long as she might have Georgy sitting by her." Walked from Brompton "in any weather" and embraced Mrs. Veal "with tearful gratitude for the delightful evening she had passed," when company retired and Georgy departed with Rowson.

**Fate of Veal's Endorsements**: Narrative comment—"Thus it seemed to be decreed by fate that Georgy was to domineer over everybody with whom he came in contact, and that friends, relatives, and domestics were all to bow the knee before the little fellow. It must be owned that he accommodated himself very willingly to this arrangement. Most people do so. And Georgy liked to play the part of master and perhaps had a natural aptitude for it."

## Georgy's Dominion at Russell Square (Chapter 24, Excerpt 1423)

**Grandfather's Fear**: In Russell Square, "everybody was afraid of Mr. Osborne, and Mr. Osborne was afraid of Georgy." Boy's "dashing manners, and offhand rattle about books and learning, his likeness to his father (dead unreconciled in Brussels yonder) awed the old gentleman and gave the young boy the mastery." Old man would "start at some hereditary feature or tone unconsciously used by the little lad, and fancy that George's father was again before him." Tried "by indulgence to the grandson to make up for harshness to the elder George." People surprised at his gentleness to boy; "He growled and swore at Miss Osborne as usual, and would smile when George came down late for breakfast."

**Mastery Over Aunt and Others**: Miss Osborne, George's aunt, "a faded old spinster, broken down by more than forty years of dulness and coarse usage"—easy for "lad of spirit to master her." When Georgy wanted anything "from the jam-pots in her cupboards to the cracked and dry old colours in her paint-box" (old paint-box from when she was "pupil of Mr. Smee and was still almost young and blooming"), he took possession; "which obtained, he took no further notice of his aunt."

**Friendships and Schemes**: For friends and cronies, had "pompous old schoolmaster, who flattered him, and a toady, his senior, whom he could thrash." Dear Mrs. Todd's delight to leave him with youngest daughter, Rosa Jemima, "a darling child of eight years old." The little pair looked "so well together," she said (privately, not to folks in "the Square"), speculating: "who knows what might happen? Don't they make a pretty little couple?"—fond mother's plan.

**Emotional Indifference to Amelia**: Georgy bears separation from Amelia easily with "a number of pleasures and consolations administered to him," whilst "his mother was yearning after him at home...every hour of the day, and during most hours of the sad lonely nights." Narrative comment: "Little boys who cry when they are going to school cry because they are going to a very uncomfortable place. It is only a few who weep from sheer affection...you need not be too confident of your own fine feelings."
